title: Ethics, compliance and professionalism
exam_coverage_note: Area C (LOs 10-15) accounts for 20-25% of exam marks, the largest single area. LO15 closes it.
apm_learning_objective: Understand ethics, compliance and professionalism as the ability to work consistently in a moral, legal and socially responsible manner.
learning_outcomes: 15a) Understand the importance of continuing professional development, which should cover both knowledge, skills and behaviours, and the individual's role in identifying and addressing their own competence gaps.
15b) Knowledge of the sources of specialist advice and standards that need to be adhered to.
15c) Understand the impact of the legal and regulatory landscape on projects (such as the impact on working conditions, risk management, governance and sustainability).
where_this_fits: This is the LO about the project professional rather than the project. It connects to LO14 (the duty to speak out when you see discrimination), LO3 (responsible project management and CSR), LO2 (the sponsor and board who oversee compliance) and LO23 (regulatory change as a risk). The single idea running through it: responsibility sits with the individual. Your employer supports your CPD but does not own it, and 'I did not know the regulation existed' is not a defence in law.

key_definitions.apm_definition: A commitment to developing and maintaining the highest standards of competence and integrity. APM frames it as five things: knowledge, competence, career development, continuing professional development and professional conduct.
key_definitions.plain_english: Knowing your job, keeping that knowledge current, and behaving properly while doing it.

key_definitions.apm_definition: Learning experiences which help you develop and improve your professional practice (CIPD). It involves identifying current and future needs, setting learning objectives, planning development activities, and recording activities and achievements.
key_definitions.plain_english: Deliberately staying good at your job. Planned and recorded, not just whatever happened to come up.

key_definitions.apm_definition: Someone who actively reflects on their experiences, finding learning opportunities in daily experiences, successes, setbacks and unresolved issues rather than relying on digested knowledge such as training.
key_definitions.plain_english: Someone who learns from the work itself, not only from courses about the work.

key_definitions.apm_definition: A framework of standards guiding the development of project professionals: breadth (Body of Knowledge), depth (Competence Framework), achievement (qualifications), accountability (Code of Professional Conduct) and commitment (CPD).
key_definitions.plain_english: Five things a professional is measured on, each with an APM artefact behind it.

key_definitions.apm_definition: The code setting standards for project professionals in four areas: professional conduct, personal responsibility, responsibility to the profession and the Association, and ethical conduct.
key_definitions.plain_english: The rulebook for behaviour. Accountability is the dimension of professionalism it sits under.

key_definitions.apm_definition: An international or industry standard an organisation elects to follow rather than being required to, adopted for reasons including risk aversion, continuous improvement or as a marketing differentiator. An example is ISO 14001:2015 for environmental performance.
key_definitions.plain_english: A standard you choose to meet. Nobody makes you; you do it because it is worth doing or worth being seen to do.

key_definitions.apm_definition: The basis on which some organisations go beyond minimum compliance, aiming to achieve or exceed the spirit of the law rather than just its letter.
key_definitions.plain_english: Meeting the intention behind a rule rather than the minimum the rule technically requires.

key_definitions.apm_definition: An organisation's defined appetite for compliance risk, alongside specific compliance objectives. A common example is a desire to 'do no harm'.
key_definitions.plain_english: How close to the legal line the organisation is willing to operate. Set deliberately, not by accident.

key_definitions.apm_definition: Speaking up to report any form of wrongdoing. A professional duty under the ethical conduct standard, with responsibilities extending beyond the professional body and carrying wider legal implications.
key_definitions.plain_english: Reporting wrongdoing. A duty rather than an option, and protected by law in many countries.

core_content.outcome_title: Continuing professional development and your own competence gaps
core_content.body_markdown:
## CPD: what it is
APM borrows its definition from the CIPD: CPD is the learning that develops and improves how you practise professionally.

APM frames professionalism as five things: knowledge, competence, career development, CPD and professional conduct. CPD is one of five, not the whole of it.

## CPD: the four ongoing activities
| Activity | What it involves |
|---|---|
| Identify current and future needs | Both of them: what you lack now, and what the work is about to require |
| Set learning objectives and targets | Turning a gap into something you can aim at |
| Plan activities | Supporting personal and professional development |
| Record activities and achievements | Which matters for maintaining formal status, and for knowing what you actually did |

## The CPD cycle: a repeating loop
A repeating loop rather than a list:
1. Reflection on practice: where are the gaps in what I know and what I can do?
2. Planning: how can I learn it?
3. Action: the learning, and putting it into practice.
4. Evaluation: what have I learned, and how is it benefiting my practice?

Then back to reflection. The evaluation step is the one that gets skipped, and it is the one that makes the difference: attending a course is not development until something about your practice changes.

## CPD ownership: three participants, one owner
This is the heart of 15a, because the syllabus asks specifically about the individual's role in identifying and addressing their own competence gaps.

| Participant | Their part |
|---|---|
| The learner | Takes responsibility for identifying their own competence gaps, and pursues learning or opportunities to fill them |
| The manager | Offers good performance feedback, helping set the direction for learning and development |
| The organisation | Supports CPD activities, which may include funded training or paid time off |

However, the responsibility lies firmly with each project professional. An employer who funds nothing has made your CPD harder; they have not made it someone else's problem.

## Knowledge, skills and behaviours: what CPD covers
The syllabus is explicit that CPD covers all three. Worth separating:

| Dimension | Example gap | How it gets closed |
|---|---|---|
| Knowledge | Not knowing how earned value works | Reading, courses, qualifications |
| Skills | Being unable to facilitate a workshop | Practice, coaching, doing it with support |
| Behaviours | Reacting badly to challenge | Reflection, feedback, deliberate change |

Behaviours are the hardest to self-diagnose, which is exactly why the manager's performance feedback matters. You cannot see your own shadow, to borrow LO12's phrase.

## Qualifications and accreditation: why they carry weight
Formal qualifications and accreditations carry real weight in a project professional's CPD. APM runs a structured ladder:

| Level | Qualification |
|---|---|
| Foundation | Project Fundamentals Qualification (PFQ) |
| Practitioner | Project Management Qualification (PMQ), the one you are taking |
| Advanced | Project Professional Qualification (PPQ) |
| Chartered | Chartered Project Professional (ChPP), the highest attainment of knowledge, professional practice and ethical behaviour, recorded on APM's Register of Chartered Project Professionals |

Other awarding bodies also offer qualifications, among them further and higher education institutions and other professional bodies, and project professionals often hold accreditations from more than one.

Maintaining status requires CPD: those holding formal certifications may need continuing CPD to keep them, and each professional body publishes its own CPD requirements, usually counted in CPD units, or professional development units (PDUs).

## Learning beyond courses: other ways to develop
Development works better when it reaches past courses and certificates. The sources named:

| Source | What it offers |
|---|---|
| Academic journals, e.g. *International Journal of Project Management* | Research findings |
| Practitioner magazines, e.g. *Project* | The profession in practice |
| Podcasts and YouTube channels | A mix of knowledge and opinion |
| Blogs and social media | Keeping up with trends and challenges |
| Conferences | Platforms for sharing and learning, and building contacts |

## The reflective practitioner: learning from experience
Reflective practitioners actively reflect on their experiences. They take their learning from the work rather than from pre-packaged training, mining the ordinary run of the job: what went well, what went badly, and what is still unresolved.

Note all four sources of learning in that list. Setbacks and unresolved issues count as much as successes, which connects to LO12's point that a leader must accept mistakes will happen and focus on what can be learned, and to LO6's lessons-learned reviews.

A project professional who only develops on training days is developing a few days a year. A reflective practitioner is developing continuously, from work they were doing anyway.

core_content.outcome_title: Sources of specialist advice and the standards to adhere to
core_content.body_markdown:
## Specialist advice: why you need it at all
A single piece of project work can reach across several industries and several countries, each carrying its own laws, regulations and standards. No individual carries that in their head, and in law, ignorance is not a defence. Knowing where to get advice is itself a professional competence.

## Specialist advice: where it comes from
| Source | When used |
|---|---|
| Organisational functions | Specialists who advise the project from within the organisation. Procurement and project finance law specialists are the examples given |
| Core project team members | Where the need is constant the specialist is embedded, such as health and safety managers on a construction project |
| External legal or consultancy advice | In an unfamiliar regulatory environment, brought in from outside |
| The sponsor and governance board | They oversee and challenge project practice, provide support, and may commission expert guidance or legal support |
| Professional bodies | APM and others publish codes, frameworks and standards |

The governance route matters and links straight to LO2: if a project needs legal support it cannot fund, that is an escalation to the sponsor, not a decision to proceed uninformed.

## The hierarchy of standards: how they stack
Standards are not a flat list. They stack:

| Level | Character |
|---|---|
| Laws | Binding. Non-compliance can carry fines or custodial sentences |
| Regulations | Binding, and often industry-specific |
| International directives | Binding depending on jurisdiction |
| Government or industry guidance | Expected practice, and may be effectively mandatory in a sector |
| Discretionary standards | Adopted by choice, for example ISO 14001:2015 for environmental performance |
| Organisational policy and procedure | The organisation's own rules, sitting inside all of the above |

Codes of practice sit within many regulatory frameworks, and can be mandatory. On top of those, organisations can elect to follow discretionary standards.

## Discretionary standards: why organisations adopt them
Three named reasons:
- risk aversion
- continuous improvement
- as a marketing differentiator

A standard can be adopted for commercial positioning rather than for its content, and both are legitimate.

## Minimum compliance vs the spirit of the law: two positions
| Position | What it means |
|---|---|
| Minimum compliance | What most organisations aim for: meeting the relevant legislation and regulations |
| Beyond compliance | Some set out to meet, or better, what the law was actually trying to achieve, as part of corporate social responsibility |

Plenty of organisations also set compliance objectives explicitly, and decide how much compliance risk they will carry, with 'do no harm' a common example. That is the same deliberate-appetite thinking as risk appetite in LO1 and LO23, applied to compliance.

## Professional standards: the FIVE Dimensions

Beyond legal and regulatory standards, project professionals are held to professional ones. The APM FIVE Dimensions of Professionalism:

| Dimension | The APM artefact behind it |
|---|---|
| Breadth | The Body of Knowledge, what you need to know to run a project of any type |
| Depth | The Competence Framework, levels of knowledge and experience, mapped |
| Achievement | APM qualifications, recognised across the profession |
| Accountability | The Code of Professional Conduct, the ethical practice expected |
| Commitment | CPD |

## The Code of Professional Conduct: four areas
Four areas, and the second of them carries most of the detail:

| Area | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Professional conduct | Being competent, acting with integrity, and respecting the law, the regulations, and health, safety and environmental duties |
| Personal responsibility | Honesty, probity, confidentiality and sound judgement; serving the interests of employers and clients. Plus keeping your CPD up, declaring any interest, turning down inducements, working with due diligence, and owning what you do |
| Responsibility to the profession and the Association | Protecting and strengthening how APM and the profession are regarded |
| Ethical conduct | Doing the right thing, and raising ethical concerns when you have them |

Rejecting inducements appears here and connects directly to LO10, where the use of rewards and coercion to influence stakeholders was said to rarely have integrity. The same principle, stated as a professional obligation.

## The duty to speak up: reporting wrongdoing
Reporting wrongdoing is a professional duty, and the ethical conduct standard says so. Speaking up is everyone's obligation. The familiar word for it is whistleblowing, and that obligation runs wider than the professional body, with legal weight behind it.

What organisations must provide:

- a policy and process enabling individuals to speak up
- legal protection for people reporting suspected wrongdoing exists in many countries, the examples given being fraud or corruption, and health and safety not being safeguarded
- that protection can cover what has happened, what is happening, and what might happen, and can extend to raising concerns about a different company, one inside the project, the programme or the supply chain

What project professionals must do:

1. Build a culture ethical enough that speaking up feels safe.
2. Make sure every team member knows the route, should they need it.

Essentially, both halves are needed. A reporting process nobody feels safe using, or a safe culture where nobody knows the route, each fails on its own. Good organisations also write down a clear set of values, communicate them, and live by them at every level where decisions get made, which is the same 'best values are the ones the team sets for itself' idea from LO12.

core_content.outcome_title: How the legal and regulatory landscape affects projects
core_content.body_markdown:
## The legal and regulatory framework: where it comes from
Every piece of project work sits inside a legal and regulatory framework. Three things shape it: the industry involved, the country the work is done in, and the country the product ends up in.

Both locations matter. A product built in one jurisdiction and sold into another inherits obligations from both.

Understanding the regulatory environment is part of the job. The law does not accept not knowing as an excuse.

## Regulation: it changes, so monitor it
The legal and regulatory picture shifts, so you need something standing that watches for those changes. Not a one-off check at the start, but a standing arrangement, staffed by qualified and experienced experts.

This is also a live link to LO23: regulatory change is a project risk with a known likelihood of occurring, and a monitoring mechanism is the response.

## Regulation: three categories
Each category demands something different of the project.

| Category | What it requires | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Prescriptive | Specific actions the project must take | Control of substances hazardous to health |
| Competence-based | Competence of key team members to be pre-established | Roles requiring certification before work starts |
| Goal-setting | Employers set goals but decide how to meet them | Manual handling operations |

The distinction is practical. A prescriptive regulation tells you what to do. A goal-setting one leaves the method to you but still holds you to the outcome, which is harder, because there is no checklist to complete.

Some regulations are specific to the type of work, construction design and management regulations for instance. Others are relevant to all work, data privacy and safeguarding people at work among them. And some situations require team members or specialist advisors to be appropriately qualified or certified for specific pieces of work.

## The regulatory environment: what it reaches into
The syllabus asks about the impact on projects, and APM names the processes affected:

| Process | How regulation shapes it |
|---|---|
| Requirements capture | Regulatory obligations become requirements, and non-negotiable ones |
| Quality planning | Standards to be met and evidenced |
| Integrated planning | Compliance activity has to be planned and resourced |
| Scheduling | Approvals, inspections and certifications take time and sit on the critical path |
| Risk and issue management | Non-compliance is a risk, and regulatory change is a risk |
| Change control | Changes must be assessed for compliance impact, not only cost and schedule |
| Project audit and assurance | What gets audited against |

Regulation is not a separate workstream; it is a constraint threaded through the existing processes.

The syllabus also names working conditions, governance and sustainability specifically:

- Working conditions: safeguarding people at work, health and safety, and the competence requirements that go with them.
- Governance: the sponsor and board oversee and challenge project practice, and compliance sits inside the governance framework from LO2.
- Sustainability: regulatory compliance is one of the named benefits of embedding sustainability in LO3, preserving the licence to operate, and discretionary standards such as ISO 14001 are adopted to improve environmental performance.

## Non-compliance: the consequences
Breach a legally binding regulation and the organisation can face corrective action or a fine. For some breaches, an individual can go to prison.

Three factors scale the sanction:

| Factor | The question |
|---|---|
| Extent and impact | How far did the non-compliance reach, and what harm did it do? |
| Individual or systemic failure | Was this one person, or the way the organisation works? |
| How it arose | Accident, oversight, carelessness or deliberate commission |

The third factor runs on a scale of culpability: an accident and a deliberate act are treated very differently, with oversight and carelessness in between.

## Conflicting jurisdictions: when laws clash
Run a project across borders and you will eventually find two sets of rules that cannot both be satisfied.

The answer: which standard the project aligns to is settled by the governance structure, on specialist advice where that is needed.

It is a governance decision, informed by specialist advice, and that is the same delegated-authority principle as LO2, applied to a decision that exceeds the project's competence as well as its authority.

exam_tips.heading: Regulation: three categories
exam_tips.tip: The three categories are directly examinable, so learn them by what each demands of you rather than by name. Goal-setting is the one to watch, because a scenario can look compliant while nobody has chosen a method.

exam_tips.heading: The regulatory environment: what it reaches into
exam_tips.tip: That table answers a 15c impact question on its own. Name three or four of the processes and say what regulation does to each, and you have covered the impact the question is asking about.

exam_tips.heading: Non-compliance: the consequences
exam_tips.tip: That last point is worth stating plainly in an answer: the consequence is not always corporate. Individuals can go to prison. The scale of culpability in the third factor is a genuinely useful thing to reason with in a scenario.

exam_tips.heading: Conflicting jurisdictions: when laws clash
exam_tips.tip: Note what that is not. It is not the project manager picking the more convenient standard, and it is not defaulting to the home jurisdiction. A scenario that hands you two conflicting rulebooks is testing whether you escalate.

worked_examples.heading: Regulation: three categories
worked_examples.situation: Manual handling on your fit-out site is hurting people. The regulation sets the goal and names no method.
worked_examples.ask: Do you wait for an inspector to tell you what to install?
worked_examples.answer: No. Goal-setting regulation leaves the method to you and still holds you to the outcome, so the assessment, the lifting aids and the training are yours to choose and yours to evidence. No checklist discharges it for you.

worked_examples.heading: The regulatory environment: what it reaches into
worked_examples.situation: A supplier offers cheaper cladding that saves 48,000 pounds and two weeks. Your change board meets Thursday.
worked_examples.ask: Is that a cost and schedule decision?
worked_examples.answer: No. Every change gets assessed for compliance impact as well, and cladding sits under building regulations. Approve it on cost and programme alone and you have taken a regulatory risk the board never saw, which is what change control exists to catch.

misconceptions.wrong: CPD is the employer's responsibility to provide.
misconceptions.right: Three parties are involved: learner, manager and organisation. Responsibility lies firmly with each project professional to identify their own competence gaps and pursue learning to fill them.

misconceptions.wrong: CPD means training courses and qualifications.
misconceptions.right: Learning is more effective when it ranges beyond formal courses into journals, practitioner magazines, podcasts, blogs and conferences. A reflective practitioner finds learning in daily experiences, successes, setbacks and unresolved issues.
The syllabus specifies knowledge, skills and behaviours. Behaviours are the hardest to self-diagnose, which is why a manager's performance feedback matters.

misconceptions.wrong: Not knowing about a regulation is a reasonable explanation for breaching it.
misconceptions.right: In law, ignorance is not a defence. Project professionals must understand the regulatory environment and establish a mechanism for monitoring changes to it.

misconceptions.wrong: All regulations tell you what actions to take.
misconceptions.right: There are three categories. Some prescribe specific actions, some require competence to be pre-established, and some set goals but leave employers to decide how to meet them.

Organisations face corrective action or fines, and for some breaches an individual can go to prison. The sanction scales with how far the breach reached and what harm it did, whether one person or the system failed, and whether it was an accident or done deliberately.

misconceptions.wrong: Where jurisdictions conflict, the project manager chooses which standard to apply.
misconceptions.right: Which standard the project aligns to is a governance decision, taken on specialist advice where needed. It sits beyond the project's competence as well as its authority.

misconceptions.wrong: Meeting minimum compliance is what good practice requires.
misconceptions.right: Minimum compliance is what most organisations target, but some go further and set out to meet or better what the law was trying to achieve, as part of corporate social responsibility and a deliberately set compliance risk appetite.

misconceptions.wrong: Speaking up about wrongdoing is a matter of personal conscience.
misconceptions.right: It is a professional duty under the ethical conduct standard of the Code, with implications beyond the professional body. Project professionals must both create a culture where it feels safe and ensure everyone knows how to do it.

misconceptions.wrong: Whistleblowing protection applies to reporting your own employer about current events.
misconceptions.right: Protection in many countries extends to past, present or potential future events, and can cover speaking up about another company, one in the project, programme or supply chain.

memory_aids.expansion: The CPD cycle. Evaluation is the step that gets skipped, and it is the one that turns a course attended into practice changed.
Learner, manager and organisation all take part in CPD. The responsibility for identifying and closing your own competence gaps sits with you.
The APM FIVE Dimensions of Professionalism, mapped to the Body of Knowledge, the Competence Framework, qualifications, the Code of Professional Conduct and CPD.

memory_aids.acronym: Do this, be qualified, hit this goal
memory_aids.expansion: The three categories of regulation. Prescriptive actions, pre-established competence, or goals with the method left to you.

memory_aids.acronym: Safe to speak, and know how
memory_aids.expansion: Both halves are needed. A reporting process nobody trusts fails, and a trusting culture with no known route fails too.

progress_checkpoint: I can define CPD, give the four stages of the CPD cycle, and explain what each stage asks.
I can name the three participants in CPD and explain where responsibility for competence gaps actually sits.
I can explain what a reflective practitioner does differently, and name learning sources beyond formal courses.
I can name the sources of specialist advice available to a project and say when each is used.
I can describe the hierarchy of legal and regulatory influences and explain why organisations adopt discretionary standards.
I can name the APM FIVE Dimensions of Professionalism and the four areas of the Code of Professional Conduct.
I can give the three categories of regulation and name the project processes the regulatory environment affects.
